question: As part of its European Green Deal, the Commission pledged to phase out the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in Europe and to significantly reduce the EU’s agricultural dependence on synthetic pesticides by implementing integrated pest management.

In stark contrast with these promises, 37 approved active substances listed as PFAS have been excluded from the proposal on restricting PFAS under the REACH Regulation. Because of their longevity and other toxic properties, these substances, which are deliberately released into the environment and then build up in crops, pose a threat to human health and the environment.

A new report shows that this PFAS risk has not been sufficiently addressed by the current implementation of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009 and that the use of these substances, at least in France, has increased spectacularly over the last 10 years. 1.
Does the Commission agree that PFAS pesticides are an unacceptable source of PFAS pollution that must be phased out?
If so, to manage risk, will it reconsider the blanket derogation proposed in the PFAS restriction for active substances used in pesticides?
Will it consider longevity as an unacceptable effect on the environment in the context of renewal procedures for these PFAS substances under Regulation (EC) 1107/2009?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.3.2024) The Commission would like to recall that the EU legislation on plant protection products1 (Regulation (EC) 1107/2009) is among the strictest in the world.

Only active substances which have no harmful effects on human health and no unacceptable effects on the environment can be approved for use in plant protection products (PPP) and Member States can only authorise plant protection products if they also fulfil these conditions.

In the restriction proposal related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under the REACH Regulation2, the four Member States and Norway who submitted the proposal3 did indeed exempt active substances used in PPP as they considered that Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, which requires a full risk assessment before approval of active substances, should address the concern of PFAS used in PPP.

In fact, for each active substance, including also those that are PFAS, it is assessed whether the substance or its metabolites are persistent and whether they are bioaccumulating and/or toxic. Active substances that are persistent, bioaccumulating and toxic, or very persistent and very bioaccumulating cannot be approved.

The Commission has recently initiated an exchange of views with Member States in order to understand if there are already discussions in place at national level for active substances that are identified as PFAS but nevertheless meet the current approval criteria in Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.
